sents.text: Welcome to NammaSpace: a pipeline that turns ordinary photographs of an indoor space into an explorable 3D digital twin.
A digital twin is a faithful, measurable 3D copy of a real place. Anyone can open it and walk through it in a web browser, with no headset and no app to install.
In this Round One prototype, we reconstruct a real indoor environment, and explore it freely on the web.
To summarise: COLMAP camera poses, OpenMVS dense reconstruction and meshing, compressed glTF, and a three.js viewer with first-person free roaming. All open source, and all running in the browser.
Next, we will capture our own spaces with a smartphone using the same pipeline, and add semantic labels, measurements and indoor navigation, turning digital twins into spatial intelligence.
This was NammaSpace. Thank you.
For this prototype we use a public research dataset, not our own capture: the Dr Johnson scene from Deep Blending, published by Hedman and colleagues at SIGGRAPH Asia 2018.
It contains two hundred and sixty-three overlapping photographs of a historic house interior, with COLMAP camera poses, as distributed with the 3D Gaussian Splatting benchmark.
Our pipeline is fully open source, and ran on a laptop CPU. OpenMVS estimates a depth map for every photograph, and fuses them into a dense point cloud of 2.1 million points.
A Delaunay graph-cut step turns those points into a surface mesh, which is textured from the original photographs, and compressed for the web.
These are the real intermediate results, inside our viewer. First, the sparse structure-from-motion points, with every camera position.
Next, the dense multi-view stereo point cloud.
Then, the reconstructed surface mesh.
And finally, the textured digital twin.
This is the NammaSpace web viewer, built with three.js. In Explore mode, dragging the mouse orbits around the entire reconstruction.
The ceiling is cut away automatically, so the layout of the house reads like a floor plan.
Scrolling the mouse wheel zooms in, so we can inspect details: the paintings, the furniture, and the doorways between rooms.
Double-clicking any surface flies the camera to it, and right-dragging pans the view.
The About panel lists the data source and the real statistics of this reconstruction run. And the viewer can switch to fullscreen.
Now for the most important part: free roaming. Switching to Walk mode places us inside the house, at eye height.
W, A, S and D move, and dragging the mouse looks around, just like a first-person game. The overlay in the corner shows the keys being pressed.
Movement is collision-aware. A BVH-accelerated raycast against the mesh stops us from walking through walls, and lets us slide along them instead.
The minimap shows our live position and heading on the reconstructed floor plan.
We can walk out of one room, through the doorway, and into the next. Every surface we see was reconstructed from the photographs.
Holding Shift moves faster, and Tour mode replays the original camera trajectory, recovered by structure from motion.
